title: Sourdough Focaccia Topping Ideas: Using a Scraper for Dimpling
meta_description: Elevate your sourdough focaccia with creative topping ideas and a pro tip on how to dimple sourdough focaccia using a dough scraper for deep pockets.
html:
There is something deeply satisfying about a slab of sourdough focaccia. The tang of the wild yeast paired with a golden, olive-oil-crisped crust makes it the ultimate side dish or snack. However, the real magic happens in the dimples. Those little craters aren't just for looks; they are designed to hold pools of olive oil and your favorite toppings so they don't just slide off during the bake.

If you've ever struggled with a dough that springs back or fingers that get too sticky, you might be wondering how to dimple sourdough focaccia more effectively. While most recipes tell you to use your fingertips, there is a secret weapon in the kitchen: the dough scraper. Using a scraper allows you to create deeper, more consistent pockets without deflating the entire loaf.

The Secret Technique: How to Dimple Sourdough Focaccia with a Scraper

When your sourdough has had its final proof in the pan and is glistening with olive oil, it's time to dimple. Instead of just pressing down with your fingers, try using the edge of a dough scraper. This is where a high-quality tool makes a difference. I personally recommend the 3-in-1 Sourdough Whisk Set (Whisk, Scraper, Lame) because the scraper is sturdy enough to push through the tension of a high-hydration dough without tearing it.

To do this, hold the scraper at a slight angle and press firmly into the dough in a grid pattern. This creates a structural "well." Once you've established these deeper pockets, you can go back in with your fingertips to add those classic, smaller dimples around the edges. This hybrid method ensures that your toppings—like heavy olives or cherry tomatoes—stay put and don't migrate during the oven spring.

Savory Topping Combinations for Sourdough Focaccia

Once you've mastered the dimpling process, it's time to load up. Because sourdough has a more complex, acidic flavor than commercial yeast bread, it can handle bolder toppings. Here are a few of my favorite combinations:

  • The Mediterranean: Halved cherry tomatoes, Kalamata olives, thinly sliced red onion, and a sprinkle of dried oregano.
  • The Garlic Herb: Freshly minced garlic, chopped rosemary, and a heavy dusting of flaky sea salt (Maldon is a great choice here).
  • The Sweet & Salty: Thinly sliced Granny Smith apples, crumbled gorgonzola, and a drizzle of honey immediately after baking.
  • The Roasted Veggie: Thinly sliced zucchini rounds and red bell pepper, pressed deep into the dimples so they roast in the oil.

Using Your Sourdough Kit for the Perfect Prep

Great focaccia starts long before the dimpling. The consistency of your dough determines how well it holds those pockets. If your dough is too slack, the dimples will vanish; if it's too tight, they won't form. This is why I suggest the 3-in-1 Sourdough Whisk Set (Whisk, Scraper, Lame) for beginners. The Danish dough whisk is a game-changer for mixing high-hydration focaccia dough without the mess of a traditional spoon.

The whisk allows you to incorporate the flour and water quickly, while the scraper helps you perform your stretch-and-folds on the counter. By the time you get to the final pan proof, your dough will have the strength and elasticity needed to make the most of your dimpling technique.

Common Mistakes When Dimpling Your Dough

The biggest mistake most home bakers make is dimpling too early. If the dough hasn't fully proofed in the pan, it will simply spring back up, erasing all your hard work. Wait until the dough is jiggly and has visible bubbles on the surface. If you press in and the hole closes immediately, give it another 30 minutes.

Another common error is neglecting the oil. You want a generous layer of olive oil on top of the dough before you start. This lubricates your fingers (or your scraper) and ensures that the toppings fry in the oil rather than drying out in the heat of the oven. If you're using the scraper from the 3-in-1 Sourdough Whisk Set, just give the tool a quick dip in oil first for a smoother glide.

Baking and Finishing Touches

Preheat your oven to 425°F (220°C). For an extra crispy bottom, bake your focaccia on the lowest rack or even directly on a preheated baking stone. As the bread bakes, the dimples you created will act as little reservoirs, trapping the oil and the juices from your toppings.

Once it comes out of the oven, resist the urge to cut it immediately. Let it rest for at least 10 minutes on a wire rack. This prevents the bottom from becoming soggy and allows the internal structure to set, ensuring every slice has that perfect, airy crumb.

FAQ

Why do my dimples disappear after baking?

This usually happens if the dough was under-proofed or if you didn't use enough olive oil. When the dough hits the heat, it undergoes "oven spring." If the gluten is too tight, it will push back up. Ensure your dough is fully relaxed and bubbly before you begin dimpling.

Can I use a dough scraper on all types of bread?

Yes! While we're talking about focaccia, a dough scraper is essential for folding sourdough, cleaning your workspace, and dividing dough into equal portions. It's one of the most versatile tools in a baker's kit.

What is the best oil for focaccia toppings?

Extra virgin olive oil is the standard for flavor, but for a higher smoke point, some bakers use a blend of EVOO and avocado oil. The key is to be generous; the oil is what creates that signature fried-bread texture on the bottom.
